Content

CELL

  • The study of cell is called: Cytology.
  • Cyto: Cell
  • Logy: Study
  • Cell is:
  • Building blocks of life.
  • Fundamental unit of life.
  • Structural and functional basis of life.

Discovery of Cell

  • Dead cell: Robert Hooke (in cork) → Father of Cytology (1665).
  • Living cell: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (in pond water) in 1674.

Cell Theory

  • In 1838, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann formulated the cell theory, stating that all living organisms are composed of cells, and the cell is the basic unit of life.
  • In 1855, Rudolf Virchow published his famous Cell Theory "omnis cellula e cellula", which means new cells are formed from the pre-existing cells.
  • Largest cell in human (by volume): Ovum (female sex cell / egg).
  • Smallest cell in human body: Sperm (male sex cell; ~5 µm head).
  • Largest cell in human body by length: Neuron (nerve cell; also the longest cell — axons can reach >1 m).
  • Smallest cell in human body (in females): RBC (red blood cell ~7-8 µm; smaller than the ovum).
  • Largest cell (animal kingdom): Ostrich's egg.
  • Smallest cell: Mycoplasma (bacteria; ~0.1-0.3 µm).

What happens to a cell when placed in a solution?

TypeDescriptionEffect on CellSolute vs Solvent
IsotonicNormal solutionNo change in cell sizeSolute = Solvent
HypotonicDilute solutionCell swells (turgidity)Solute < Solvent
HypertonicConcentrated solutionCell shrinks (plasmolysis)Solute > Solvent

Turgor pressure causes enlargement and extensive growth of cells.

Parts of Cell

Cell Membrane

  • The cell membrane is also called the plasma membrane.
  • It is a thin, elastic, and flexible structure.
  • It is the outermost covering of the cell in animal cells (in plant cells, it lies just beneath the cell wall)

Functions:

  • It acts as a protective barrier → like a bodyguard.
  • It gives shape to the cell.
  • It holds and protects the internal contents.
  • It controls movement of substances in and out (acts as a selectively permeable membrane) → Composition: Proteins (50%) + Lipids (50%).
  • Phospholipids
  • Cholesterol

Movement across Cell Membrane

  • Diffusion: Spontaneous movement of molecules from higher to lower concentration.
  • Rate of Diffusion: Gases > Liquids > Solids. E.g. Diffusion of agarbatti smell.
  • Osmosis: Movement of water (solvent) from a region of higher water potential (lower solute concentration) to lower water potential (higher solute concentration) through a semi-permeable membrane. Cell absorbs water through osmosis, no energy is required and it lasts up to equilibrium state.

Solution = Solute + Solvent

Active Transport/Reverse Osmosis

  • Movement of molecules across a cell membrane from a region of lower to higher concentration. It requires cellular energy.

Cell Wall

  • It is only present in plant/bacteria/fungus/algae.
  • The cell wall is not a living structure.
  • The cell wall allows the free passage of molecules, unlike the selectively permeable cell membrane.
  • It provides rigidity and shape to the cell.
  • It offers structural support and protection to the cell.

Materials of Cell Wall:

  • Bacteria: Peptin/Peptidoglycan.
  • Fungi: Chitin.
  • Plant: Cellulose.
  • Algae: Cellulose/Pectin.

Glycocalyx: A surface layer (slime layer) that covers the cell membrane in bacteria.

Chromosomes

  • Chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus of cells that contain DNA and genes.
  • They carry genetic information from cell to cell.
  • Components of Chromosomes: DNA and Proteins (Histones).
  • Total: 46 Chromosomes (23 pairs) in a human being.
  • 22 pairs (autosomal)
  • 1 pair (sex pair): XX (female) and XY (male).

DNA

  • DNA carries genetic information, and genes, which are functional segments of DNA, are responsible for transmitting this information from one generation to the next.

CELL

  • DNA molecule discovery: Friedrich Miescher (1869).
  • Double-helical structure by: Watson and Crick (1953).

Cytoplasm

  • Cytoplasm is the fluid that fills up the cells. It is the part that is located between the plasma membrane and nuclear envelope.
  • Cell organelles are present in cytoplasm.
  • Cytosol: The aqueous (water-based) fluid portion of the cytoplasm.
  • Cytoplasmic Inclusions: Non-living components (pigments, nutrients, etc.) of cytoplasm. It exists in two forms: Euchromatin and Heterochromatin.
  1. 1. Euchromatin: Loosely packed, transcriptionally active.
  2. 2. Heterochromatin: Tightly packed, transcriptionally inactive.
  • During cell division, chromatin condenses to form chromosomes.

Nucleus

  • Nucleus is known as "Brain of the Cell", it controls the activities of different cell organelles.
  • Discovered by: Robert Brown in 1831.
  • The nucleus is found in the center of the cell.
  • The nucleus is the largest organelle (double-membraned) in a eukaryotic cell.
  • The nucleus is enclosed by a double-layered nuclear membrane, which separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm.
  • It permits materials between nucleoplasm and cytoplasm.

Nucleoplasm

  • Nucleoplasm is a type of protoplasm (the term coined by Purkinje in 1839) that is composed of thick fluid and constitutes chromatin fibres made up of DNA and usually found in the nucleus of the eukaryotic cells.

Contents of Nucleoplasm:

  1. 1. Nucleolus: The nucleolus is a distinct, non-membrane-bound structure within the nucleus of eukaryotic cells, primarily known for its role in ribosome biogenesis.
  2. 2. Chromatin material: Chromatin is the complex of DNA and proteins, primarily histones, that makes up the genetic material of the cell.

Bacterial Flagellum

  • Flagella are microscopic hair-like structures involved in the locomotion of a cell.
  • The flagella is a helical structure composed of flagellin protein. The flagella structure is divided into three parts: Basal body, Hook, and Filament.
  • Basal Body: It is attached to the cell membrane and cytoplasmic membrane.
  • Hook: It is a broader area present at the base of the filament.
  • Filament: Thin hair-like structure arising from the hook.

The protoplasm is the living material of the cell and composed of biomolecules like nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates.

Types of Cell: Prokaryotic cell and Eukaryotic cell.

Prokaryotic CellEukaryotic Cell
Size: 1-10 μmSize: 10-100 μm
Nucleus absentNucleus present
Nucleolus absentNucleolus present
Cell organelles is absentCell organelles present
Chromosome: singleChromosome: more than one
E.g. Bacteria, Cyanobacteria (Blue green algae), mycoplasmaE.g. Plant and animal cell

CELL ORGANELLES

  • Cell organelles are specialized, membrane-bound structures within cells that perform specific functions essential for cell survival and function, much like organs in the body.

Mitochondria

  • Length: 1-2 um (1 micro metre: 10⁻⁶ m).
  • Diameter: 0.1-0.6 um.
  • Mitochondria is involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death).
  • It is also known as "Powerhouse of the cell" responsible for ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) synthesis to make energy. ATP is also called as energy currency of the cell.
  • Two membranes: Outer membrane (porous in nature) and Inner membrane (responsible for ATP synthesis).
  • Mitochondria has its own DNA and ribosomes.
  • Shape is like a "sausage".

Ribosomes

  • Ribosomes do not have membrane.
  • They are essential cell structures for protein synthesis.
  • Discovered by: George E. Palade (1955).

Endoplasmic Reticulum

  • They are network of sac-like structures.

CELL

  • They are attached to plasma membrane on one side and outer nuclear membrane on the other.
  • Endoplasmic Reticulum serves as transport between cytoplasm and nucleus.
  • Detoxify poisons, and drugs (SER in liver through an enzyme Cytochrome P450).
  • Types: Long tubules, Vesicles, and Cisternae.

Functions:

Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum

  • It is characterized by ribosomes on its surface, which are responsible for protein synthesis.

Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum

  • It is characterized by the absence of ribosomes and plays a crucial role in synthesizing lipids and fats. Ribosomes are absent here.

Golgi Bodies

  • Discovered by: Camillo Golgi (1898).
  • It consist of vesicles, cisternae, and vacuoles.
  • Golgi bodies has two distinct faces:
  • → Cis face: Convex, faces towards the nucleus (receiving side).
  • → Trans face: Concave, faces towards plasma membrane (mature/shipping side).

Functions:

  • It responsible for packaging and despatching of proteins and lipids (also known as "Post Office" of the cell).
  • It is involved in forming complex sugar from simple sugars.
  • It forms lysosomes.

Lysosomes

  • It is known as "suicide bag of the cell".
  • Lysosomes are filled with digestive enzymes (made in RER) that acts as waste disposal system of cell.
  • When the cells get damaged, lysosomes may burst leading to enzymes digesting their own cell.

Vacuoles

  • Vacuoles are membrane bound solid or liquid filled sac-like structures.

In plants:

  • They are large and distinct and occupy significant portion of cell volume (50-90%).
  • They store cell sap.
  • They provide turgidity and rigidity to the cell.
  • In plant cells, vacuoles are generally considered permanent, large, and central structures.

In animals:

  • In animal cells, vacuoles are smaller, more numerous, and often temporary.
  • They store glucose, glycogen, and protein.

Cell sap consists of:

  • Amino acids
  • Sugars
  • Organic acids

Peroxisomes

  • It breakdowns very long chain of fatty acid through beta oxidation.
  • It contains oxidative enzymes (E.g. Catalase) that convert harmful hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. It acts as free radical scavengers, helping to detoxify the cell.

Plastids

  • Plastids are only present in plant cell and not in animal cell.
  • It has its own DNA and ribosomes.

Types:

  1. 1. Chloroplast
  • Chloroplasts are green plastids that contain chlorophyll, the pigment responsible for photosynthesis.
  • They also contain yellow and orange pigments like Xanthophylls and Carotenes.
  • Chlorophyll molecules contain magnesium (Mg²⁺), which is essential for capturing solar energy during food synthesis (photosynthesis).
  1. 2. Chromoplasts
  • Chromoplasts contains different types of pigments, which provides colour. E.g. Red colour in tomato which is due to lycopene, red colour in chilli which is due to capsanthin.
  1. 3. Leucoplasts
  • Leucoplasts are colourless plastids, mainly involved in storage.

They are of three types:

  • Amyloplast: Storage of carbohydrates.
  • Aleuroplast: Storage of proteins.
  • Elaioplast: Storage of fats.

Cell Division

  • Cell division is the process where a parent cell divides into two or more daughter cells.

Reason for division:

  • Growth of organism.
  • To replace old, dead, and injured cell.
  • Gamete formation (Meiosis).

Mitosis and Meiosis

CELL

MitosisMeiosis
Occurs in somatic cells (body cells)Occurs in germ cells (reproductive cells)
The nucleus divides only onceThe nucleus divides twice
Produces two daughter cellsProduces four daughter cells
Daughter cells are diploid (2n) → same no. of chromosomes as the parent cellsDaughter cells are haploid (n) → half the no. of chromosomes as the parent cells
Cells are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cellCells are genetically different from each other and from the parent cell
Responsible for growth, repair, and asexual reproductionResponsible for formation of gametes (egg and sperm cells)
No genetic variation occursGenetic variation occurs due to crossing over and independent assortment
Malfunction can lead to cancer (uncontrolled cell division)Malfunction can lead to genetic disorders such as: Down's syndrome, Klinefelter's syndrome, Turner's syndrome

Cell Cycle

  • **G1 Phase (Gap 1):** The cell grows and performs its normal functions, preparing for DNA replication.
  • **S Phase (Synthesis):** The cell replicates its DNA, creating two identical copies of each chromosome.
  • **G2 Phase (Gap 2):** The cell continues to grow and prepares for mitosis, ensuring that DNA replication is complete and that the cell is ready to divide.
  • Mitotic Phase: This phase involves the division of the cell's nucleus and cytoplasm.

Cytoskeleton

  • Cytoskeleton helps in providing structural support to cell.
  • Cytoskeleton helps in cell movement.

Centrosome

  • The centrosome is responsible for organizing microtubules, which are essential for cell structure, movement, and division.
  • Each centriole is a cylindrical structure made up of microtubule triplets arranged in a 9+0 form (nine peripheral triplets with no central microtubules). Cilia and flagella, by contrast, have a 9+2 arrangement (nine outer doublets plus two central singlets).

Microtubules

  • Microtubules are hollow, cylindrical structures composed of tubulin proteins that form part of the cell's cytoskeleton, providing structural support, facilitating cell movement, and playing a crucial role in cell division.

PLANT VS ANIMAL CELL

Plant CellAnimal Cell
Cell wall is presentCell wall is absent
Chloroplast is present for photosynthesisChloroplast is absent
Almost rectangular in shapeSmall, irregular, or round in shape
Large vacuoles are presentSmall vacuoles are present
Plastids are presentPlastids are absent
Has less number of mitochondriaHas more number of mitochondria
Reserve food material starchReserve food material is glycogen

DNA REPLICATION IN ANIMALS

DNA replication is a process by which cell makes an exact copy of its DNA before cell division. This ensures that each new cell gets the same genetic information.

Enzymes Essential for DNA Replication in Animal Cell

  • Helicase: This is an unwinding enzyme. It "unwinds" or "unzips" the double-stranded DNA.
  • Topoisomerase: This enzyme prevents DNA from getting tangled (avoid supercoiling).
  • DNA Primase: This enzyme initiates DNA replication (new strands are produced).
  • DNA Polymerase: This enzyme doubles the amount of DNA in a cell during cell division (builder).
  • DNA Ligase: This enzyme facilitates the joining of DNA strand together (gluer).

Reverse Transcriptase: the process of creating complementary strands of DNA based on RNA.

Semi Conservative DNA Replication

  • It is the process of duplicating DNA to create two new double stranded DNA molecules, each with one original strand, and one new strand.

CELL

Endocytosis and Exocytosis

Endocytosis

  • Endocytosis is a type of active transport where a cell engulfs external materials, forming a vesicle to bring them inside.
  • It includes processes like phagocytosis (cell eating) and pinocytosis (cell drinking). E.g. Entrapment of food particles by Amoeba.

Exocytosis

  • Exocytosis is a cellular process where a cell transports molecules out of the cell by using vesicles that fuse with the cell membrane, releasing their contents into the extracellular space.
  • It is also known as cell vomiting. Vomited particles are undigested residues from endocytosis → enzymes and hormones.
